item.title: The Unrelenting Nightmare of Applying to High School in New York City
item.description:
Until recently, I thought my worst New York City experience was the time I was waiting to cross Houston Street and a cackling vagrant punched me in the face. That, however, was before I started the process of getting my oldest kid into a public high school.

New York has an almost purely school choice system; most families don’t have a default high school that they’re zoned for. The admissions process, a mix of meritocratic culling and sheer chance, is time-consuming, psychologically taxing and so byzantine that it’s hard to describe to anyone who hasn’t endured it.

“I was somehow holding it together with all the balls in the air until this high school process,” Eva Pinkley, a single mother in Brooklyn, told me last week, as her neurodivergent son worked on an application essay with a coach she could barely afford. Now, she said, “I’m completely falling apart.” An education reporter I know contemplated moving out of the city after seeing high school applications up close. Friends of mine who’ve endured the process say the only consolation is that it makes applying to college seem easy.

I’d heard how miserable it was before it was my turn, but was still shocked by it, in part because of a stroke of particularly bad luck. My kid will, I think, be fine — I will go to great lengths to assure it — but I’m not sure how people with fewer resources cope. And the whole nightmare made me curious about how it got this way, and who all this punishing complexity serves.

“By many measures, New York is the kind of city where school choice is supposed to shine,” writes the Princeton sociologist Jennifer L. Jennings in her recent book about school choice, “The Scarcity Loop.” It’s huge and wealthy, with hundreds of options and good public transportation. But the problem in New York, as in most other big cities, is that there aren’t enough seats in excellent schools to go around.

So getting into high school feels like playing multiple games of musical chairs simultaneously. Places are distributed according to a bewildering mixture of lotteries, grades, tests, interviews, essays, auditions and portfolios. School choice is meant to be fairer than rationing education by ZIP code — as typically happens in suburbs — and in some ways it is. But the system in New York is a bureaucratic Rube Goldberg machine that locks out families that don’t know how to operate it while driving privileged ones crazy. It demonstrates the way school choice policies can shift responsibility for securing each kid a great education away from government and onto individuals. They trap us in a joyless competition and make us feel like it’s our fault when we lose.

“Families with institutional fluency and flexible schedules are better equipped to manage this hidden curriculum,” Jennings writes in “The Scarcity Loop.” “Others, facing language barriers or inflexible work, are filtered out by the grind itself, excluded by process rather than lines on a map. Even for savvy parents, the process leaves its mark in the erosion of evenings, weekends and mothers’ sleep.”

On New York’s high school application, families list the schools they’re applying to in order of preference. Students are divided up into five tiers based on their marks in seventh grade, and, separately, assigned a hexadecimal lottery number — really a combination of letters and numbers — that determines their priority in the city’s school-matching algorithm. (The meaning of the lottery numbers is indecipherable to laypeople, but parents in the know turn to a chart created by the computer science professor Amélie Marian, a revered figure on the school-application message boards.) Some schools take kids only from the highest tier, which can shut out those who get a single A- in seventh grade. But perfect grades are no guarantee, either, if you get a bad lottery number.

This year my son was in the top tier, but Marian’s data showed that his lottery number was among the worst possible. That means we’ll be matched to a school only after the other 99 percent of city kids are given their choices of the schools they qualify for. By then, the schools that usually take kids only from the top tier are expected to be full. So will the most desirable schools that accept kids from across the academic spectrum.

We’re hanging our hopes on the SHSAT, an SAT-like test that determines access to eight of the city’s specialized high schools, as well as a handful of other public schools with their own tests, essays and interviews. And while I respect arguments against the charter school movement — I even agree with some of them — we’ve applied to a well-regarded Brooklyn charter school and I have found myself wishing there were more.

Since none of these options are sure bets, we’re seeking out safety schools that are well run but not too selective, reasonably rigorous and, importantly, no more than an hour away by public transportation. To find them, we’ve relied on social media, word of mouth — parents we know have assembled spreadsheets — and a Zoom meeting with an embarrassingly expensive consultant. Having come up with a handful of backup schools, we’re trying to visit them during tours and open houses, though often these fill up so quickly that parents trade spots online.

Obviously, the lottery system isn’t unfair just because we got the short end of it; someone has to be last. What infuriates me is the underlying shortage of seats in schools that are challenging and well resourced, forcing parents to scratch and claw for a place, or to settle. The system creates a sense that “if it fails, it’s on you,” Jennings told me. “If you jump through the right hoops and know the secret codes at the right time, you’ll be able to get a seat.”

There’s no way to know how many families are driven out of the public school system by this ordeal. But we do know that enrollment in New York’s public schools is shrinking. In an Education Department survey released last year, 41 percent of families that withdrew from the city’s public school system said they were seeking “more rigorous” education. Forty percent departed because their families moved. Among that group, half said “concerns about schools” were one of their reasons for leaving the city. It seems obvious that the “Hunger Games” aspect of public high school admissions is a drag on New York’s fortunes, one Zohran Mamdani needs to address, though he didn’t create it.

Some of the system’s maddening features date back to Michael Bloomberg’s administration. Bloomberg closed underperforming neighborhood schools and encouraged the proliferation of small, career-focused high schools. Today, the city has lots of themed schools — there are schools for sports management, marketing and hip-hop — but not nearly enough neighborhood high schools with broad, general-interest offerings and honors tracks. Without a zoned high school, families have little incentive to lobby to make their local ones better. Ambitious kids often must resign themselves to long commutes. “High-achieving kids travel a lot farther than lower-achieving kids,” said Jennings.

Public school inequality is a wicked problem, and I won’t pretend to have an easy solution to it. Ultimately, I think part of the answer is bringing back neighborhood high schools, not as a replacement for school choice, but as a supplement. “The process is extremely stress-inducing because people feel that they don’t have agency and they don’t have predictability,” said Marian, the computer scientist. If all parents had at least one community school they could depend on, some predictability would be restored.

But that’s a long-term goal. In the short term, Mamdani’s administration, so focused on making government more responsive to its citizens, can look for ways to take some of the pain out of the application process. Here’s one small idea:

Several of the most sought-after schools ask students to submit essays about how they will both contribute to and benefit from those schools’ unique pedagogical approaches. In a system in which families are scrambling for any foothold they can find, these assignments do not encourage sincerity. They are unrewarding to write and tedious to oversee. If schools want a writing component, there should be one essay, maybe with a choice of prompts, used for all of them.

Overall, the goal should be more ease and simplicity. “Rationing always imposes work somewhere; the moral question is where that work lands, and who pays,” writes Jennings. Right now, most of the work falls on parents. The one resource this system treats as inexhaustible is families’ time.

item.title: What Makes Men in Groups Behave So Badly?
item.description:
I keep thinking about an emoji posted in a group chat of more than 50 young men: a devil’s face (😈). And a text: “This is crazy work” — which I take to mean wild, out of bounds, outrageous. These and other Snapchat messages written by members of Cornell University’s Chi Phi fraternity have provoked intense outrage on behalf of Jane Doe, who says she was sexually assaulted by seven men that night, because the misogyny on display is so transparent. “Free pussy”; “Like you can walk in and whip it out”; “Shop still open?” This, almost everyone agrees, is abhorrent behavior. It is the language of rape culture.

Why the devil emoji? I think the forbidden nature of sex with Jane Doe was part of the chat’s collective excitement. I see a tacit awareness that a severely intoxicated woman can’t consent to sex — and an insistence on going ahead anyway. Then: a shared delight that the group of brothers is getting away with it, together. The men cheered: “I fucking love chi phi”; “CHI PHIII.” Masculinity is performed, proved and reveled in: You show yourself to be big men on campus by collectively preying on a vulnerable woman.

Why do men in groups behave this way? What makes a man in front of an audience of other men offer up a woman like a piece of meat for consumption? Two of the men whom Jane Doe describes assaulting her that night were something like friends to her. In the days after, they sent messages that appeared sympathetic and caring. “I’m so so sorry,” one texted. Another wrote, “How’ve you been coping with the stress? You need anything?” These same men were the ones who advertised her body for the taking to their fraternity brothers. (All the men accused by Jane Doe have denied wrongdoing.)

I am a professor at Cornell, and a few days ago I spoke to Diego Estrada, a former student of mine who served as the president of a fraternity on campus, graduated and was working as a live-in adviser at a different fraternity in fall 2024, when news broke of Jane Doe’s allegations. I wanted to understand what the conversation was like within fraternities at the time.

Mr. Estrada described to me the mood he observed at one of the frats he thought of as socially comparable to Chi Phi. The members there overall seemed sympathetic to the Chi Phi men; they felt bad that these men were being “ruined” by what Jane Doe was saying. Their response, Mr. Estrada said, was identical to the victim-blaming comments we now see spreading online: that Jane Doe brought what happened on herself by drinking and going to the fraternity house.

He told me he was appalled by what he heard, but said nothing. He didn’t want to be seen as a scold. Nor did he want to lose his job at the time, and consequently his meal plan and housing.

My term for the sympathy shown to male perpetrators over female victims is “himpathy.” I see this insidious sentiment at work in the Chi Phi chat in the loyalty that bonds frat brother to brother, which would make any attempt to hold each other accountable feel like a betrayal. It appears that nobody who saw the group chat that night openly objected to the behavior; on the contrary, many of the men egged one another on and seemed to escalate it. At least two men entered the room where Jane Doe was after seeing the chat, and one reported back to it that she was still in there. (To be fair, one member of Chi Phi did share the Snapchat conversation, perhaps feeling enough moral compunction to document what was happening.)

The Chi Phi group chat fits into a clear pattern of men subjugating women as a way of bonding with other men. According to the norms within many all-male groups, when one man proposes doing something immoral or illegal, the bro code dictates that other men go along with it. Sociological research has shown that one of the ways men demonstrate their masculinity to one another is through misogynistic sexual violence, as well as aggression and coercive control of women.

It’s easy to see, then, how male group dynamics can turn toxic all too quickly: One particularly entitled or cruel man decides to prey on a vulnerable woman, and invites other men to participate. They feel not only excited but even honor bound to take up that invitation. A 2007 study found that men who join fraternities are three times as likely to commit sexual violence during their freshman year, even though they were no more likely to have committed assault beforehand. That data has since been further supported. Frats appear to have the power to take men and turn them into rapists.

A secondary rule of the bro code is that you don’t call out another man’s bad behavior or intervene to protect the victim. A fraternity brother has a strong sense of duty to protect and uplift his own. And he in turn feels entitled to loyalty from his brethren. After Jane Doe’s allegations came out on campus, one of the accused men complained to another that he felt abandoned by Chi Phi. “Talking about ‘brotherhood’ and then no one except a couple real ones check in, much less acknowledge our existence,” he wrote. “Dead ass bro,” was the response. These men felt sorry for themselves. They even felt like victims.

I recently read a report titled “Campus Gang Rape: Party Games?” that analyzed more than 50 cases of gang rape on university campuses of all kinds: Ivys, small liberal-arts colleges, state schools. It identified a pattern:

A fraternity holds a party. In many cases … a young woman often has had too much to drink and/or too many drugs. Therefore she may be unaware that the “friendly” persuasion of the brothers is actually a planned pursuit of easy prey. By the time she recognizes her predicament, her confusion has changed to fear and panic, and escape seems impossible. She is unable to protest or her protests are ignored. Anywhere from two to eleven or more men rape her.

The report was published over 40 years ago, in 1985. What is new in the case of Jane Doe is that old patterns of sexual predation are being enabled and facilitated in terrifying ways by modern technology. Groups of men can now form and coordinate with far greater ease than they could in any previous era. They can invite one another to commit rape from behind the anonymizing shield of their screens. Online, the misogyny and rape culture that can foment within all-male spaces operates on a grand scale, at the speed of light.

The effects of this are evident far beyond the university. In France, Dominique Pelicot recruited upward of 50 men from a website to rape his drugged wife. An Italian Facebook group devoted to trading nonconsensual photos of wives and girlfriends numbered in the tens of thousands. This year a CNN investigation reported on a chat room in which men from around the world shared strategies for, and videos of, drugging and assaulting their partners; one French lawmaker referred to such groups as online rape academies.

Even in the more mundane corners of the internet — gaming, YouTube, social media — we find groups of men congregating to air their resentments toward women and plan sexual exploitation. In September, Wired wrote about Maddie Kowalski, a university student who was recorded during sex acts without her consent. The videos were circulated on Snapchat, where they were picked up by an online doxxing community and further disseminated on X. The videos, with Ms. Kowalski’s name attached, were ultimately viewed millions of times. The devastating impact on her and other women who have been similarly victimized can hardly be overstated.

The internet is where young people come of age, and it is soaked through with such misogyny. Perhaps this is why sexual violence has not diminished in the post-#MeToo era. Indeed, at Cornell sexual violence appears to be increasing. The university’s 2025 survey data showed that 35 percent of female undergraduates had experienced some form of sexual assault during their time at Cornell, compared with 23 percent in 2023.

Last week, Michael Kotlikoff, Cornell’s president, suspended fraternity parties until the end of the school year. But ultimately this policy is likely to be as successful as Prohibition was in ending alcohol consumption: Parties will be driven underground while Greek life remains in operation.

Ban the frats, I say, and Mr. Estrada, the former frat president, almost agrees with me. But he is struck by how he feels when he says it: guilty, ashamed, as if he is betraying his brethren in even contemplating their dissolution.

He told me that his girlfriend asked him recently what he would have done if he’d been part of the Chi Phi group chat that night. He was characteristically honest and insightful in his reply. “I was thrown off by my internal response because immediately what I thought of was, well, am I still fraternity president?” he said. “It’s kind of terrifying. That’s how much it’s been drilled into me, as president, that my job is to protect my brothers and defuse the threat, versus the need to be a good person.”

As the mother of a 14 year old boy, how do I best make sure he at least understands this dynamic? It starts with self awareness. And then I can only hope he will take the right actions when he is put in a similar situation. I found the discussions with Mr. Estrada the most interesting. What do the bystanders do? I don’t think my kid would be an instigator. But I could see how he may remain silent. Or want to defend his friends. This is the dynamic we need to fight.

It’s not just frats anymore, but banning them would be a good start. Men need to seriously consider how they bond with other men in all kinds of groups and recognize that “bro code” is just misogyny enforced by bullying, emasculation, and violence. Until there is systemic change, all men’s groups are sus.

Not to excuse those guys, who were criminals and disgusting, but I think the more interesting question is "why do *humans* in groups behave so badly?Just look at the current administration. It is perfectly possible for a group to be mixed-gender and do some pretty repellent things. I suspect the same dynamics of group belonging are at work.

Kate Manne, a moral, social and feminist philosopher at Cornell University, is the author of “Entitled,” “Down Girl” and “Unshrinking” and writes the newsletter More to Hate.

item.title: Can New York Win the War on Rats?
item.description:
Good morning. It’s Tuesday. Today we’ll find out about the newest weapon in the never-ending war on rats in New York City. We’ll also meet the new president of Pace University, coming from a position as a top official at Texas A&M.

Your first reaction to the latest weapon in New York City’s war on rats might be: Hasn’t somebody tried this before?

Somebody did — private exterminators, including one hired with $10,000 allocated by the City Council to clear rats from a block on the Upper East Side in 2023. Now the parks department is using the same weapon, a machine that shoots carbon monoxide into rats’ burrows in curbside tree beds.

“The rats get drowsy, and they fall asleep — permanently,” explained Danny Hernandez, an administrative parks and recreation manager.

He said that this poses less collateral risk than poison, which he said puts birds, pets and potentially children at risk. The machine that pumps in the carbon monoxide uses an oil to make the otherwise invisible gas visible. That lets people know where it is, and even so, there are restrictions. The device can only be used outdoors, and it can’t be used within 10 feet of a residential building.

Rats are a perennial problem in New York, something that standup comedians joke about. They’re funny until you see one yourself, in your very own neighborhood. Former Mayor Eric Adams — who fought tickets for rat infestations at a townhouse he owns in Brooklyn — called them “Public Enemy No. 1.” He also appointed a “rat czar” in 2023 who left the administration quietly in 2025.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani does not appear to share his predecessor’s preoccupation with rats.

What about the larger question: Who’s winning, the humans or the rats?

My colleague Dodai Stewart says that’s hard to figure out.

No one knows how many rats live in New York City. It’s not as if there’s a rat census every 10 years. She says that it’s easier to count the humans who have complained about rats.

So far this year, New Yorkers have filed 25,025 rodent complaints with 311. That’s the fewest recorded for the same period in the seven years of data analyzed by The New York Times.

But the 311 data has its shortcomings. The app for rodent complaints wasn’t working for nine months between last year and this year. Some neighborhoods are more attuned to calling 311, while others seem to shrug. And the way information is channeled through city agencies has changed over time, complicating year-to-year comparisons.

Caroline Bragdon, the Health Department’s director of neighborhood interventions for pest control services, prefers building inspection data. As the pandemic waned, inspectors spotted a lot of rats out and about. Now the number of properties that fail inspection is “beginning to decline,” she said. “We think, long-term, we’re going to see success in continued declines.”

The Sanitation Department has credited a change in “rat-human interactions” for some improvement. That mostly refers to rats’ interactions with humans’ garbage.

The dynamic has changed in the not quite two years since the city began requiring businesses and many buildings to put trash in sealed bins instead of loose bags. The rats were primed to scour sidewalks and curbs for four-star meals: They had developed longer noses and shorter upper teeth than their ancestors in northern China and Siberia, according to a 2024 paper in the journal Science.

Several city agencies are fighting the rat war. The Sanitation Department continues the effort to get bagged garbage in containers. The Health Department conducts inspections for rat activity, based on complaints, and posts a color-coded map in its department’s Rat Information Portal.

And the parks department has a team of six people to neutralize rats in what Hernandez, watching the crew with the carbon monoxide machine, estimated are 600,000 to 700,000 tree beds.

“It would take us 150 years to hit every tree bed in New York,” he said with a sigh.

Weather

Today will be sunny with a high near 69. The sky will be mostly clear tonight with a low near 48.

ALTERNATE-SIDE PARKING

In effect until Nov. 1 (All Saints’ Day).

QUOTE OF THE DAY

“A lot of us do point to his words.” — Gisella Castagna, a Barnard College student who attended a screening of the documentary “Edward Said: Between Worlds,” about the Palestinian American literary critic and activist who taught at Columbia University for decades.

Expanding 2-K: Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced that the city would expand free child care for 2-year-olds to Staten Island and across the Bronx by adding 10,000 seats next school year. Wealthier neighborhoods in Manhattan and Brooklyn will not get any new 2-K seats.

Vintage bus: A restored version of Volkswagen’s Flower Power-era Microbus, by Kindred Motorworks, is newly fitted out with electric power. The vintage bus caused a lot of heads to swivel on a leisurely tour of Bergen County, N.J.

Subway shooting victim: Officials identified the man who was shot and killed inside the Seventh Avenue station at 53rd Street on Saturday as Darrel Rodriguez, 26, who grew up in the Bronx and worked as a security guard. No arrests have been made.

Life after a layoff: Two years ago, Janald DuFont was working as a creative project manager for Ebony magazine, earning about $100,000 a year, and living in a “semi-luxury” building in Bedford-Stuyvesant, Brooklyn. Now he’s back living in his childhood bedroom. Here’s how he’s living on $30,000 a year as a comedian and production assistant.

Pace University is hiring Robert Ahdieh, a top official from Texas A&M University, as its next president. He grew up in Jackson Heights, Queens, and says that Pace’s motto — “Opportunitas,” Latin for “opportunity” — has personal resonance.

His parents emigrated from Iran, his father in the late 1950s and his mother in the mid-1960s. “It’s not all universities that center opportunity in their motto and their mission,” he said.

Ahdieh, 55, will replace Marvin Krislov, the president since 2017, who said in February that he was not seeking another five-year term. Ahdieh will take office on Jan. 1.

He said that Pace could capitalize on its location, with most of its 13,000 students attending classes in Lower Manhattan. “The opportunities it creates for internships and externships, that drives outcomes and success,” he said. Pace is “not New York University, it’s New York’s university.” (Pace also has campuses in Pleasantville and White Plains, N.Y., in Westchester County.)

Ahdieh, who has a law degree from Yale, was a trial attorney in the civil rights division of the Justice Department and taught at Emory University for 18 years before he was named dean of the Texas A&M law school. Texas A&M later gave him two additional titles — vice president for professional schools and programs in 2022, and chief operating officer in 2023.

In April Texas A&M named a new president, Susan Ballabina, who had been the executive vice chancellor for the A&M system. When asked if he was in the running for the job, Ahdieh said, “Not as such,” adding that Ballabina was “a no-brainer for the role.”

Texas A&M is building a presence in Fort Worth, 170 miles from its main campus in College Station, Texas. The project was initially intended to provide a new home for the law school, which Ahdieh said had occupied a former telephone company switching facility. But he said the plans grew, with an eye toward providing A&M with “a significant urban platform” and Fort Worth — “the largest major city in the country that didn’t have a large Tier 1 university” — with an academic and industry hub for different disciplines.

Pace noted in a statement that enrollment at the law school had grown from 458 students to more than 2,000 during Ahdieh’s years there, and the percentage of students who passed the bar had climbed from 73 percent to nearly 100 percent.

METROPOLITAN diary

Dear Diary:

I was standing on a packed subway train on my way into Manhattan when I overheard two women having a lively conversation.

“I just don’t eat pork anymore” the louder of the two said. “See here? Pork chop scar!”

“What do you mean?” the other woman asked, turning to get a look at her friend’s face.

“Right here,” the first woman said. “My right brow bone. See? Look closely!”

I couldn’t resist trying to get a peek myself as her friend leaned in for a closer inspection.

“Like how?” the second woman said in amazement.

“One day, when I was a teenager, I came home from school absolutely starving,” the first woman said, “and I peered over my mother’s shoulder as she was in the midst of seasoning some T-bone chops for the grill.”

She then recounted the exchange that followed:

“‘What’s for dinner tonight, Mom?’

“‘Pork chops,’ she replied.

“‘Oh no, not pork chops again!’

“Thwack! Pork chop scar!”

— Jacqueline Rush Lee

Illustrated by Agnes Lee. Tell us your New York story here and read more Metropolitan Diary here.

Glad we could get together here. See you tomorrow. — J.B.

Davaughnia Wilson and Ed Shanahan contributed to New York Today. You can reach the team at nytoday@nytimes.com.

item.title: What It Took for Nikole Hannah-Jones to Write About Her Daughter’s Distress
item.description:
“Should I have written this?”

In her 23-year career as a journalist and Pulitzer Prize winner, Nikole Hannah-Jones had never asked herself that question before. Then again, she told me, she had never written a piece as personal and vulnerable as her September article in The New York Times Magazine, “In Fighting For Every Child, Did I Betray My Own?”

The 8,000-word piece grapples with the consequences of her and her husband’s decision to enroll their daughter, Najya, in predominantly Black, low-income schools in New York City. The article is a follow-up to one Nikole wrote 10 years ago about Najya, who is now a teenager — and who now disagrees with her parents’ schooling decisions for her.

To write the piece with integrity, Nikole said, she had to lay herself bare — and, in doing so, exposed herself and her daughter and effectively handed ammunition to critics of hers and her choices. So for a quick minute, as she read some of the online criticism of the article, she wondered if it was worth it.

I recently spoke with Nikole about that, what went into writing the piece, readers’ reactions and whether she agreed with any of the criticism. Our interview has been edited and condensed for length and clarity. (A slightly more condensed version of the interview is available as a video.)

PATRICK HEALY: You had to make the decision about whether to put a very public spotlight on your daughter. How did you go about making that decision?

NIKOLE HANNAH-JONES: With the original essay, I had never intended to write about our family’s experience. But then our school became embroiled in this national integration fight. I had been covering these issues since my first job, and it seemed impossible not to write about it.

So I pitched it, and my editors were very excited about it, and then I immediately regretted the original pitch because I’m like, man, I have to expose my child. Where I ultimately came down — I am always writing about other parents, children who are struggling through these issues of school segregation. And it almost felt hypocritical that, when it came to my own family, I would say this is the one case where we have to not tell the story of a child.

PATRICK: Many people have trusted you over the years to tell their stories. What is it like having your daughter put that kind of trust in you? What is that sense of responsibility like?

NIKOLE: Heavy. To me, it felt like a matter of integrity. When I wrote the first piece 10 years ago, so many people responded to that story, that story meant so much to them. And here was my child saying, I had a different experience. And so, as a journalist, as just a person who tries to walk through the world with integrity, I felt I had to be honest about how it went. What were the struggles? Were we able to hold the line? And what were the impacts on the person who was on the cover of that magazine?

PATRICK: When you think about the educational choices that you were making for Najya, do you feel like you made the right choice?

NIKOLE: I love that you’re asking that because I actually think, no offense, that’s the wrong question.

PATRICK: Yeah, tell me.

NIKOLE: That’s a question that has been so much of the focus since the piece came out — is whether this one family’s choice for their one child was right or wrong. To me, the question is, why do we abide a system that forces this choice?

And that’s really what I wanted us to question, to say, you know, even a parent who has all of these resources was getting crushed by the system of inequality. So if it can crush me, what do you think it’s doing to our most marginalized children? That, to me, is really the question.

I will never regret that we made a decision that we wanted to try to struggle alongside our community. I grew up in a very working class family. I spent my first few years in segregated, high-poverty schools. It’s very personal to me that children do not deserve to be robbed of an opportunity to receive an education because their families don’t have resources. And that everyone who can leave shouldn’t leave. I believe that strongly. So I think the choice was right. My mistake and my regret is not taking enough into account how it would and that it did affect my child in a negative way.

PATRICK: Were there details you started putting into the piece and then thought — that’s too much, or, I don’t want to go there?

NIKOLE: Pretty much all the examples that I thought were important ended up in the story. I was worried that with some of the examples I wanted to use, Najya would say, I really don’t want that published. And if she had told me that, I would have respected that. That’s no different than how I treat any child whose stories I’ve told. But there wasn’t anything that she disagreed with.

All I kept saying to myself as I was writing it was, I know I am giving people ammunition, I know the critiques that are going to come with it, and yet I have to be truthful. So even if that truth is very unflattering to me, I feel like we get into this to try to tell the truth and that has to include yourself if you’re going to put yourself out there.

PATRICK: Was there any part of the criticism of the article or of you that you agreed with?

NIKOLE: I mean, of course. It would sound crazy if I’d say none of the critique was valid. But I’m like, what is the critique? So can you critique my parenting? Sure, join the club, right?

And then there’s some critique that I think is just a misreading of what I was arguing. So I’ve seen the critique of, like, I had the hubris to think one person could change New York City public schools. Never say that, never believe that — in fact, I say the opposite. The critique that, you know, it was naïve. It wasn’t naïve. I knew what to expect. It didn’t make it easier, but I knew to expect it. And then, of course, the conservative critique, which is that this is an argument for school choice, which I adamantly push back on, because New York City is a system of school choice. And school choice is actually what has led to the inequality. And any other critiques of me personally, I don’t care.

PATRICK: Yeah, you’ve been to that rodeo before.

NIKOLE: Well, yeah, and also, what does it matter? Like what someone thinks about me personally, that’s not really relevant to what the journalism is trying to do. I guess there were some people who felt I didn’t spend enough time talking about high-achieving Black high schools. Valid. You’re not a journalist worth your salt if you’re not constantly assessing the little things you didn’t get right or looking back at your writing and wishing you had done things better.

There was some online discourse that was pretty brutal. And, you know, I have experienced some brutal discourse through the years, but usually not about me as a parent. That was hard. And for a minute, I’m like, man, should I have written this? And I’ve actually never, ever as a journalist questioned should I have written something. And there was a moment where I was just like, I did not have to subject myself to this. Should I have done this? I can’t regret that either. You know, in the end, I’m fine. I will be fine. My feelings got a little hurt because I’m a human being, but in the end, people are talking about these kids who don’t have a platform, who don’t have a choice.

The mayor of New York has been forced to respond, has now promised to release a plan to address it. That doesn’t happen without me writing a piece like this. It is the power of what we can do with our platform, and what I would argue is our responsibility to do.

PATRICK: One thing we hear from readers about Times journalism is, why do you write about this and not that? I’ve heard from some readers about your piece saying, I would have been more interested if there had been more about teachers unions and kind of the role of them and quality. Do you try to anticipate readers’ expectations for a piece while also thinking, I have an intent for doing it this way?

NIKOLE: That’s a good question. I have lots of thoughts on the teachers’ union, but I’m not going to dump one sentence in there that doesn’t deal with the complexity. No piece can do everything. I mean, this is why I’ve been writing about school segregation for 20 years. If you could just write one story, and that one story told us everything that we needed to know, you’d never need to write about it again. So I would just hope that readers read something like this with more curiosity and less certainty.

PATRICK: Part of the honesty of the piece is that uncertainty — that there aren’t easy answers. I wonder, during the writing process, if you felt like, maybe I need to be leaning more into black and white? Or if you felt like the ambiguity is where the truth is?

NIKOLE: I think that I feel ambiguous myself. I’ve been covering this for so long. There’s been so little change, sustained movement. I’m ambiguous on, do we really actually care? And will we ever actually do something? And, in ten years, will my own child feel differently than she feels today? Ten years ago when I wrote the first piece, I put that question in there, right? Like, one day my child is probably going to question this choice and I won’t know how to answer it, and I still don’t know how to answer it, except it was worth the try. We should have tried. We all should try more.

PATRICK: I love that answer. I want to push you on one part of the answer.

NIKOLE: Push me. C’mon.

PATRICK: Can we care and yet not know what —

NIKOLE: What to do? Yes.

PATRICK: How do people reconcile that? How do policymakers reconcile that? How do you build a constituency, or even, dare I say, like a consensus around what to do?

NIKOLE: I can never give a sound bite answer to this because it is complex, but, you know, we’re all complicit in these structures of inequality. It doesn’t mean we agree with them, but we’re also not really doing anything to end them. And many of us actually take advantage of them or we benefit from them. That is why, ultimately, if we’re going to change this it has to be at a policy level, it has to be from leadership on top. It’s not going to come from individual parents. You may be able to go into a school. You may be able to change a school, but you’re not going to change the system.

So, I think, what I tried to put forth in this essay is a woman who was humbled, right? Is a woman who still believes in the rightness of what I tried, but also said, man, was it hard. And I don’t know that I got it quite right. No, actually, I know I did not get it quite right because my child has told me this.

]]>

item.title: Woman Who Says She Was Raped at Cornell Sends Message to Faculty Senate
item.description:
The former student who accused seven men of sexual assault in a lawsuit that has rocked Cornell University wrote in a letter to faculty leaders last week that she felt “unsupported” and “disbelieved” by the school’s president, Michael Kotlikoff.

In a two-page letter to the faculty senate, the former student, known as Jane Doe, said she had wanted to share a “secondhand account” as the senate considers a rare vote of no-confidence in Dr. Kotlikoff’s administration. The letter described a comment she said he had made in a meeting with students and administrators shortly after she alleged she had been raped at a fraternity house.

His “initial response,” she wrote, “was along the lines of, ‘Why did she wait so long to report it?’”

The alleged assault occurred on Oct. 19 and 20, 2024. She went to the campus police about three weeks later, on Nov. 8.

The former student wrote in a letter to faculty leaders that her experience “diminished her confidence” in the administration’s ability to take her allegations seriously.

A Cornell spokeswoman said that while Dr. Kotlikoff had made a similar comment at the January 2025 meeting, the “secondhand account” was incorrect and the words had not been directed at the former student.

“The question ‘Why did it take so long for the assault to be reported?’ was directed at bystanders who did not use Cornell’s anonymous tip line, despite ongoing social media activity about the incident in October 2024,” the university said in a statement. “He was not questioning Jane Doe’s reporting.”

The former student, now 22, stopped short of telling the faculty senate how it should vote in her letter, but she said that Dr. Kotlikoff’s words, as told to her, had shaken her trust in Cornell.

“It diminished my confidence in the administration’s ability to approach my experience with the understanding, sensitivity and fairness I had hoped for and expected from what had been my dream school,” she wrote.

Her letter, obtained by The New York Times and authenticated by her lawyer, was dated Oct. 14, 2026, two weeks before the faculty senate is scheduled to begin its vote. The letter shows how the woman, who dropped out of Cornell after the alleged assault, is actively trying to weigh in on the roiling debate around her claims.

“She believed that this was important information that the faculty should know when considering what steps to take” in relation to Dr. Kotlikoff, said Thomas P. Giuffra, her lawyer.

While the faculty senate has no power to remove officials, a no-confidence vote would be a strong rebuke of Dr. Kotlikoff, who has had the support of Cornell’s powerful board of trustees in the face of some calls for his resignation. The senate will meet to debate the no-confidence resolution on Oct. 28, with voting continuing for several days after.

Mr. Giuffra sent the letter on behalf of Jane Doe to Samuel Mayer Nelson, the speaker of the faculty senate, and Chris B. Schaffer, the dean of faculty. It was unclear how many of the approximately 135 members of the faculty senate had seen the letter by Tuesday afternoon.

Early Tuesday morning, Dr. Schaffer sent an email to faculty senators acknowledging that he had received Jane Doe’s letter, and relaying the administration’s rebuttal to it. He described the contents of her letter broadly, and did not include it as an attachment.

“The dean of faculty office does not have the investigatory capacity to properly follow up on private communications of this kind, nor is this the role of the office,” he wrote to the senators, adding that the rebuttal from the administration had come from a “contemporaneous account of the meeting from a university official who was present.”

Dr. Schaffer wrote that he had forwarded the letter to Cornell’s lawyers, as well as the special investigative team, headed by Sally Yates, a former deputy attorney general, that Cornell had appointed to further examine the case and the university’s broader response to sexual assault issues.

Ariana Kim, a co-sponsor of the faculty no-confidence resolution, said she was concerned that the faculty dean still had not shared Jane Doe’s letter with her or the wider senate nearly a week after receiving it.

“It echoes and cements the feelings many of us are already having, about Cornell wanting to keep things as quiet as possible,” she said.

Cornell has faced intense criticism for its handling of the former student’s allegations in the weeks since she filed a lawsuit against the university; the Chi Phi fraternity and seven of its former brothers; and her sorority, Delta Delta Delta.

In the lawsuit, Jane Doe claims she was given drugs and gang raped over several hours in the Chi Phi fraternity house. All of the men have denied wrongdoing and none have been charged with a crime.

When the former student reported her allegations to the campus police a few weeks later, a Title IX investigation was triggered.

The meeting the former student referred to in her letter took place in January 2025 and included representatives of many of Cornell’s sororities as well as Dr. Kotlikoff and at least one other administrator, according to a person with direct knowledge of the meeting who spoke on the condition of anonymity to reveal details of a private meeting.

According to a Cornell official familiar with the matter, the conversation took place at a meet-and-greet for Dr. Kotlikoff as he was getting to know student groups during his time as interim president. The official Cornell account comes from contemporaneous notes from the meeting taken by the other administrator.

In the letter, the former student recounts the exchange that she said she was told happened between Dr. Kotlikoff and the president of her sorority. She wrote that her sorority sister relayed the conversation to her “with concern.”

“She interpreted his question as an expression of doubt in the veracity of my story,” Jane Doe said in the letter.

The sorority president said other faculty or staff members had heard the conversation, according to the letter, and that “at least one of them appeared distressed” by the president’s comment.

“When the then-Tri Delta president relayed this conversation to me, I felt unsupported and disbelieved by President Kotlikoff,” the former student wrote. “I am sharing this account now because, to my knowledge, only a few individuals are aware of the conversation; I do not know if you or other members of the faculty senate are among them.”

She added, “I would not want to withhold something potentially pertinent, only for senate members to later discover that information relevant to their deliberations had not been made available to them.”

The former president of the Cornell chapter of Tri Delta declined to comment.

Dr. Kotlikoff has said he was not aware of the details of the former student’s case after her initial report, but has stressed that he took its claims of drug and alcohol fueled abuse seriously enough to create a presidential task force on campus sexual assault in February 2025.

Cornell ultimately barred the fraternity from campus, expelled two of the accused men and suspended two others. The other three men accused by the former undergraduate received lighter punishments.

At about noon on Tuesday, Ms. Yates sent an email to students, faculty members and alumni of Cornell to reassure them of her independence as she undertook her inquiry and to ask for any relevant information they might have to share.

“We also know that a lot of people are counting on us — counting on us to speak the truth; counting on us to be fair; counting on us to get this right,” she wrote. “We will devote everything we have to live up to those expectations.”

She said that the board of trustees had pledged to provide her team with full autonomy and that the board planned to publicly release the results of her review and recommendations.

Hurubie Meko and Andrea Barnes contributed reporting.

item.title: College Football Superlatives
item.description:
Good morning! It’s already the midway point of the college football season. My alma mater did not have a football team, as I’ve probably mentioned, so all this is a little new to me.

I am getting a bit of a crash course from my colleagues at The Athletic, who are handing out midseason superlatives. Miami was named the best team; James Madison was deemed the best team from a non-Power 4 conference; Jeremiah Smith, a wide receiver for Ohio State, was named the best player; and Oregon State’s Jesse Legree was called “college football’s biggest surprise.”

Read more superlatives here, and see The Athletic’s ranking of every team.

Already over football? It’s almost basketball season. Florida was at the top of The Associated Press’s preseason poll, followed by Duke, Illinois and Connecticut.

We’re also covering:

Origins of life

The Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show

Deep fried eggs

What you need to know to be the smartest person in class today.

1. France extended its curfews. The country’s prime minister said the measures helped keep the calm overnight after days of rioting and looting.

2. Mahmoud Khalil appealed to the Supreme Court to stop his deportation. Khalil had recently graduated from Columbia University when he was arrested by ICE and became the face of the Trump administration’s crackdown on pro-Palestinian demonstrations.

3. Residents of Alberta voted to remain a part of Canada. They rejected a campaign to try to separate the oil-rich province from the rest of the country. Prime Minister Mark Carney welcomed the result.

4. Christiane Amanpour said she was leaving CNN. Amanpour, one of the most famous names in broadcast news, is stepping down next year. She started at CNN in 1983.

5. How did life arise on Earth? Three moments may offer some clues. I’m trying not to get too existential.

What you’re eating.

Avocado toast may be a millennial delicacy, but the fruit is full of nutrients. Here’s what Amelia Kingsley, 19, a chemistry major at Yale, does with them:

What are you eating? A whole avocado.

Where? In the library, in class or in the dining hall.

Her hack: I keep a stash of whole avocados in my dorm. In the morning I put one in a jar in my bag so it doesn’t get crushed, adding it to dining hall salads for extra nutrients and healthy fats.

Submit your meals to Dining Hall.

The City University of New York raised $312 million in donations during the 2026 fiscal year. My colleague James Barron talked to the chancellor to learn more.

David Sabatini, a prominent scientist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology who was forced out of his job over sexual harassment allegations, won a defamation case against his accuser, along with a $6 million award.

The vibes were high during Cornell University’s homecoming tailgate, but as nighttime came around, the effects of the party ban led to a more subdued scene.

The former Cornell student who accused seven men of sexual assault in a lawsuit sent a letter to faculty leaders last week, saying that she felt “unsupported” and “disbelieved” by the school’s president. Read the letter.

Kylie Jenner walked the Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show. She wore the Fantasy Bra, a $50 million piece with thousands of diamonds on it.

Can you guess which snack has Copenhagen in a chokehold? It’s literally sliced cheese on bread with butter, known locally as a bolle med ost (bun with cheese), shortened to BMO. The city’s top bakeries are striving to perfect the snack.

Get dumped by A.I. on reality TV. Three celebrities dated A.I. avatars on a South Korean show called “My A.I. Partner: Strange Love.” One contestant went on a pool date with one, slept next to another and was dumped by a third.

Do this to get ahead.

Fry an egg. If you can’t decide between sunny side up or over easy, how about deep frying it? Egg katsu is blowing up online. Try this recipe.

Play a board game. It could be a great way to bond (or start beef) with your friends. Here are the best ones.

Eat some seaweed. It’s great for your gut, is a complete source of protein and has some vitamins, too. Now I’m craving seaweed salad!

Thanks for hanging out with me this morning. This newsletter is powered by your submissions — tell us about your classes, questions, crushes, side hustles and obsessions here.

Also: Times access is free for half of all U.S. college students through their school. Tell your friends to check if their school provides free access.

And forward this to your roommate, professor, club president or T.A. See you tomorrow!

Want more of today’s top stories? Tune in to “The Headlines,” our podcast that includes top headlines and analysis.

Any tips or feedback? I’m all ears. Email me at extracredit@nytimes.com

The editor of Extra Credit is Talya Minsberg. Scott Nelson was our photo editor.

item.title: A Matter of Values, at Cornell and Beyond
item.description:
To the Editor:

Re “Inside the Crisis Response at Cornell’s Chi Phi House” (front page, Oct. 12):

What does it take for a room full of educated young men to realize that a woman could be in danger? A Snapchat message advertising access to her body wasn’t enough.

The New York Times’s reporting on Cornell’s Chi Phi fraternity highlights a much bigger issue. One fraternity brother entered the room after seeing the message and later told investigators that everything seemed normal. He also admitted to “bantering” about it beforehand in the group chat. What is particularly disturbing is how casually the situation was treated.

This is not just a Cornell problem. It reflects a culture in which degrading women is brushed off as a joke, sexual violence is not taken seriously enough and fitting in with a group becomes more important than doing the right thing.

As a woman at a university, I’ve constantly been reminded of the precautions I should take to protect myself. Don’t drink too much. Don’t walk alone. Watch your surroundings. But why aren’t we putting that same energy into addressing the attitudes and behaviors that make women feel unsafe in the first place? We need to stop treating sexual violence as something women are responsible for preventing and start questioning how we are raising young men.

Real change starts long before college, with teaching boys to respect women, recognize harmful behavior and hold one another accountable. This isn’t just a problem for universities to solve. It’s a problem with the values and attitudes our society continues to normalize.

Sarah GalatasAtlantaThe writer is a graduate student of social work at the University of Georgia.

To the Editor:

Just because fraternity members call each other “brothers” does not mean that The New York Times has to do the same in its reporting. With numerous reports of sexual assaults at fraternities on campuses — more than in non-Greek spaces — it is abundantly clear that many fraternity members across the country do not treat women well.

Jane Doe was a sorority member, which in Greek life meant she was a sister to the brothers at Chi Phi. What brother would participate in such an abusive group chat about his sister? The undisputed behavior of the “brothers” at Chi Phi at Cornell was beastly and ugly, even if not found to be criminal. In no definition of the word did these men treat Jane Doe as their sister.

Ruth DellTiburon, Calif.

To the Editor:

Re “Want to Address Sexual Assault? Make Fraternities Coed,” by Michael S. Roth, the president of Wesleyan University (Opinion guest essay, Oct. 17):

I was particularly struck by Dr. Roth’s observation that at Wesleyan people who see someone in a vulnerable position are now more likely to speak up. That change may be as important as any institutional reform he describes.

For many years, as an artist and the founding president of the nonprofit Have Art: Will Travel!, working with educators and curriculum scholars, I have been exploring a related question: Can we teach people to move from being bystanders to becoming upstanders?

Through art exhibitions, student discussions and a yearly $5,000 Upstander Award recognizing people who intervene on behalf of others, I have seen how important it is not merely to condemn harmful behavior but also to make intervention itself visible, discussable and valued.

Dr. Roth’s experience suggests that upstander behavior is not simply a quality some courageous individuals happen to possess. Institutions can help create cultures in which people feel both empowered and responsible to act.

Universities should ask not only how they can prevent people from causing harm, but also how they can prepare the rest of us to refuse to stand silently by when harm occurs.

Linda SteinNew York

To the Editor:

Re “Where Was the Courage at Cornell?,” by David French (column, Oct. 14):

Debates rage about what causes events similar to what happened at Cornell. Mr. French got it right; it’s what didn’t happen at Cornell that matters.

Even young men whose brains are said not to be fully formed until around age 25 can be challenged and encouraged by their college to do the right thing when bad things happen. As Mr. French points out, the courage and decency to say “Stop” wasn’t present, which he ascribes to a lack of virtue.

In ancient Athens, virtue was a constant theme of discussion in the agora of Socrates, Plato and Aristotle. We need more of that kind of discussion at our colleges — perhaps in a class of ethics, which I suggest ought to be an undergraduate course requirement. Such a class should link discussion about personal and group responsibility, care, respect, diligence and even brotherly love.

Conrad EbersteinGlen Allen, Va.

To the Editor:

Re “Avalanche of G.O.P. Cash Keeps the Party Competitive Despite Its Problems” (news article, nytimes.com, Oct. 16):

Millions of voters can outvote billions of dollars of American oligarchs’ propaganda. Let’s hope we do.

Martin S. KaplanNew York

]]>
